title: Part One, Chapter 9: The Defeat of Cabracan

verses.t: And the third who grew proud, the second son of Vucub-caquix, who was called Cabracan (that is, two legs), said, "I am the one who destroys the mountains." And likewise Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque say that they defeated Cabracan. And Huracán, Chipa-caculha and Raxa-caculha spoke, and they say that they spoke to Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque: "Let the second son of Vucub-caquix be destroyed as well; this I command, for what he does on the earth is not good, for he goes too far in his greatness, and it must not be so. Flatter him and lead him over there, towards where the sun rises." This is what Huracán said to the two boys. "Very well," they said. "Is it not right, this that we see? Is not your greatness first, you, Heart of the Sky? Am I not [your servant]?" This is what the boys said, answering what Huracán had said to them. And at that moment Cabracan was shaking the mountains; he barely moved them a little, stamping his feet on the ground, and at once the small and great mountains split apart. And then the two boys met him and asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" "I am not going anywhere," he said. "I am here only throwing down mountains, and I shall go on throwing them down for ever." And then Cabracan said to Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque, "What have you come for? I do not know you, nor do I know why you have come. What are your names?" "We have no names," they said. "We are only blowgun hunters and bird-limers in the hills. We are poor and have nothing; we wander through the great and small hills. Over there where the sun rises we saw a great mountain; its sweetness is very fragrant, and it is so high that it rises above all the mountains, and so, since it is so high, we have not been able to catch a single bird. And if it is true that you throw down mountains," said Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque, "now you will help us." "That is true," said Cabracan. "Have you seen this mountain you speak of? Where is it? I shall see it and throw it down. Where did you see it?" "Over there," they said, "it is, where the sun rises." "Very well," said Cabracan. "Come, take the road." "It must not be like that; we must take you between us, one on the right hand and the other on the left, because we are carrying our blowguns, and if there is any bird we shall shoot it." And so they went along happily, shooting at the birds (and it should be noted that when they shot, the pellet was not of clay; they brought down the birds with their breath alone), and Cabracan went along amazed. Then the boys made fire and began to roast the birds over it; and they smeared one bird with "tizate"; they put white earth on it. "This one we shall give him," they said, "when his desire grows strong, as he smells its fragrance. This bird of ours shall overcome him; and they smeared it with earth because, once overcome, he must fall to the earth and be buried in the earth. (Great and wise is the Creator,) when the creatures were brought to light." This is what the two boys said. And they said to each other, "Cabracan will long in his heart to eat it." And then they turned the bird over the fire, and it began to cook; it was already golden, and the fat dripped from the birds, and a very fragrant smell came from them. And Cabracan was most eager to eat them; his mouth watered, and drool and spittle fell from him because of the fragrance that came from the birds. And then he asked, "What is this food of yours? Its smell, which I smell, is truly delicious. Give me a little." So he said, and then a bird was given to Cabracan for his destruction. And as soon as he had finished the bird, they went on and arrived where the sun rises, where that great mountain was. And by then Cabracan was already limp, with no strength in his hands and feet, because of the earth they had smeared on the bird he ate; and he could do nothing more to the mountains, nor throw them down. And then the boys tied his hands behind him, and his feet as well, both of them, and then they threw him to the ground and buried him. And so Cabracan was defeated by Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque alone. It is not possible to tell all the deeds of these boys here on the earth.
Now we shall tell the birth of these two, Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque; for so far we have told only how Vucub-caquix, with Sipacua and Cabracan, were defeated here on the earth.
